title: Indian Chemist Gautam Desiraju Wins Crystallography's Highest Honor, the Ewald Prize
excerpt: The IISc professor emeritus and grandson of India's second President is recognized for pioneering crystal engineering over a five-decade career.
body:
• Indian chemist Gautam R. Desiraju has been awarded the 14th Ewald Prize by the International Union of Crystallography, widely considered the field's highest honor after the Nobel Prize.
  • Desiraju is recognized for pioneering crystal engineering and demonstrating how weak hydrogen and halogen bonds shape molecular crystals and biological systems.
  • He is the grandson of India's second President, Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, and earned his PhD from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1976.
  • Desiraju serves as professor emeritus at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and holds positions at IIT Mandi, Rishihood University, and UPES Dehradun.

Gautam R. Desiraju, one of India's most decorated scientists, has been awarded the 14th Ewald Prize by the International Union of Crystallography (IUCr), recognizing his foundational contributions to crystal engineering over a career spanning nearly five decades.

The Ewald Prize, established in 1986 and awarded every three years, is widely regarded as the highest global honor in crystallography and structural chemistry, short of the Nobel Prize. It commemorates Paul Ewald's contributions to the discipline and to the founding of the IUCr.

"The Ewald Prize is widely considered the highest accolade that a structural chemist or biologist can receive, short of the Nobel Prize. What stands out is the complete professionalism of the process."

— Gautam R. Desiraju

A Career Built on Weak Bonds

Desiraju is honored for his pioneering studies showing that even very weak chemical hydrogen bonds among atoms play a critical role in how crystals form. His 1989 book, Crystal Engineering: The Design of Organic Solids, remains a landmark text that provided the first comprehensive definition of the field. He coined the term "supramolecular synthon" for repeating patterns found in crystal structures that serve as building blocks for new materials — a concept paper cited nearly 3,400 times.

His body of work includes more than 475 research papers with over 80,000 citations and an h-index of approximately 105, placing him among the most highly cited structural chemists in the world, according to the IUCr.

From Illinois to Bengaluru

Desiraju earned his PhD from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1976. After conducting research at the Eastman Kodak Company in Rochester, New York, he returned to India in 1978 — at a time when the country lacked basic diffractometers for experimental crystal analysis.

Rather than seeing the limitations as obstacles, Desiraju embraced the comparative study of known crystal structures, searching for structural patterns that would eventually define crystal engineering as a discipline. He built his career at the University of Hyderabad and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, where he now holds the title of professor emeritus.

He also served as President of the International Union of Crystallography, further cementing India's presence in global scientific leadership.

A Distinguished Lineage

Desiraju is the grandson of Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, India's second President, in whose honor the country celebrates Teachers' Day on September 5. Beyond his scientific achievements, Desiraju has engaged deeply with Indian Knowledge Systems and classical music, delivering lecture-demonstrations on the compositions of Muttuswami Dikshitar at academic conferences including a recent one at IIT Mandi.

He currently holds distinguished professorships at the University of Petroleum and Energy Studies (UPES) in Dehradun and the Centre for Indian Knowledge Systems at IIT Mandi, and was recently appointed Dean of the Sajjan Agarwal School of Technology at Rishihood University.

What It Means for Indian Science

The recognition adds to a growing list of international honors for Indian scientists in 2026. Earlier this year, physicist Deepak Dhar won the Dirac Medal for his work in statistical physics. Desiraju's prize highlights India's deep bench in the physical sciences, particularly in fields where patient, decades-long research — rather than headline-grabbing breakthroughs — drives fundamental understanding.

For India's academic institutions, the recognition underscores the value of retaining world-class researchers domestically. Desiraju's decision to return to India in 1978, when facilities were sparse, and build a globally influential research program from Hyderabad and Bengaluru, offers a template that the country's expanding IIT system and new universities are actively trying to replicate.
